analysis.one_liner: Requires private insurers, employer plans, Medicare, Medicaid, and veterans' care to cover a federal schedule of preventive health services.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees and six subcommittees in 1993 and never received a vote before the Congress ended in early 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to create an annual schedule of recommended preventive care — checkups, screenings, counseling — and required nearly every kind of health coverage to pay for it: private insurance and employer plans, Medicare, Medicaid, Department of Veterans Affairs care, federal employee plans, and care for military dependents. Insurers that failed to comply would have faced a federal excise tax of up to 25 percent of the premiums they took in. It also funded county clinics for people who couldn't pay and on-site health workshops at workplaces.
analysis.who_benefits: Insured patients, Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, veterans, federal employees, and military dependents would have gained first-dollar coverage for preventive services under a uniform national schedule. Uninsured people in the 50 participating counties would have gotten free preventive care at clinics, and employees at 30 participating companies plus federal workers would have gotten on-site health promotion workshops.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients with insurance, Medicare, Medicaid, and veterans

how_it_helps.text: Every carrier and employer health plan would have to cover the preventive services applicable to each enrollee under the HHS schedule, enforced by an excise tax of up to 25 percent of premiums for noncompliance, with a $100-per-person-per-day penalty for individual-level failures [S2] [S3].
Medicare would have counted the preventive services as covered 'medical and other health services,' and Medicaid coverage would have been made mandatory, effective January 1, 1994 [S2] [S3].

Veterans, federal employees, and dependents of uniformed-service members would have gained coverage of the same preventive services, with care provided on an outpatient basis where possible [S2] [S3].

A five-year demonstration program would have funded preventive care for people unable to pay in 50 counties chosen to span urban, rural, and suburban areas, plus grants for 30 employers and on-site workshops for federal employees covering nutrition, smoking cessation, back-injury prevention, and stress management [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers offering health plans would bear the cost of covering the mandated services, backed by an excise tax on carriers of up to 25 percent of premium revenue for plans that failed to comply. Medicare, Medicaid, VA, federal employee, and military health programs would bear the added federal cost, and taxpayers would fund the county demonstration grants and workplace programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and federal health programs

drawbacks.text: Mandating coverage for a broad, annually updated schedule of services would raise premiums for insurers and employer plans, and those costs would flow to employers and workers through higher premiums [S2] [S3].

The excise tax reached 25 percent of all premium revenue for a noncomplying plan — a penalty so large it functioned as a hard mandate, and critics of coverage mandates argue they raise premium costs and can price some small employers out of offering coverage at all [S3].
Making Medicaid coverage mandatory would have imposed new costs on states, though states could delay compliance until after their next legislative session [S3].

The schedule-setting process included 'representatives of manufacturers of prescription drugs' and health plan administrators among the required consultants, alongside physicians and nurses, giving affected industries a formal seat in writing the coverage list [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — uniform first-dollar coverage of evidence-based preventive care across nearly every insurance program in the country — was real and would have reached tens of millions of people, though the evidence on preventive care reducing overall health spending is mixed: screenings often cost more than they save in treatment. The enforcement design was blunt (a tax on up to 25 percent of premium revenue), and the schedule-writing process gave industry representatives a formal consulting role. On balance the bill's benefits ran to ordinary patients and its costs to insurers, employers, and federal and state budgets.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in four House committees and was passed down to six subcommittees, but none ever voted on it, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Benjamin Gilman introduced the bill on January 5, 1993, the opening day of the 103rd Congress [S1] [S5].
The same day it was referred to four committees: Energy and Commerce, Post Office and Civil Service, Veterans' Affairs, and Ways and Means [S5].

Over the following six weeks each committee sent the bill to a subcommittee — Health, Hospitals and Health Care, Compensation and Employee Benefits, Commerce Consumer Protection and Competitiveness, and Health and the Environment [S5].
Rep. Hamilton Fish was added as an additional sponsor on May 24, 1993, making two Republicans the bill's only sponsors [S3] [S4].
The sponsor gave introductory remarks on the floor five times between January and May 1993, but no committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, and no vote was ever taken [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers came out ahead: they never faced the coverage mandate or the excise tax of up to 25 percent of premiums. Patients never gained the mandated preventive coverage, and the 50-county free-clinic demonstration never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers, who avoided the mandate

sides.party_line_note: The only two sponsors were New York Republicans, and no member of either party moved the bill past committee; the 103rd Congress's bigger health care fight dominated the session and this bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill would have forced every carrier to cover an annually updated schedule of preventive services and imposed an excise tax of up to 25 percent of premium revenue for noncompliance. Avoiding that mandate and tax is what insurers and plans stood to gain from the bill's death.

Employer health plans were directly covered by the mandate, adding benefit costs, though federal grants were available to 30 employers for voluntary on-site wellness workshops. Blocking the bill spared them the coverage requirement.

industries.industry: Doctors, clinics, and other health care providers
industries.note: Mandated coverage and the county clinic grants would have steered paying patients and public funds toward preventive care visits. More covered screening means more reimbursed services for providers.

Medicaid coverage of the schedule would have been mandatory, raising state costs, though states could delay until after their next legislative session. Beneficiaries would have gained the covered services.
